newsitem.title: USA: Jesse Jackson advises Clinton on racial issues.
newsitem.headline: Jesse Jackson advises Clinton on racial issues.

text.p: Civil rights leader Jesse Jackson appealed to President Bill Clinton on Wednesday to use an upcoming speech on race to pledge more judgeships for minorities and convene a conference on equal opportunity.

Jackson and Wade Henderson, executive director of the Civil Rights Leadership Conference, met with Clinton and his chief of staff, Erskine Bowles, for about an hour to discuss a June 14 address the president will make at the University of California at San Diego.

"We look forward to that address with great anticipation," Jackson told reporters after the meeting. "We hope that the matters that we have raised represent promises made and will become promises fulfilled and we can all be a part of the growth Americans are now realising."

Jackson said Clinton needed to nominate an assistant attorney general for civil rights and appoint a White House liaison to the African-American community. He asked for a White House conference on equal opportunity.

He said Clinton should appoint more women and minorities to some of the large number of vacant federal judgeships. He appealed to Clinton to hire more minorities for openings in federal agencies, and urged him to apply pressure for better enforcement of the country's anti-discrimination laws.
He said many women and people of colour were being left out of the country's economic expansion.

"If these agencies are adequately staffed, funded and laws vigorously enforced, that will open up opportunities, and every time opportunities are made available, the net result is growth," Jackson said.

A White House spokesman, Joe Lockhart, said Clinton was in the "consultative phase" of getting ready for a speech in which the president "wants to put issues of race and racial recognition front and centre so we can deal with them effectively."
"We very much appreciate Jesse Jackson's input and his input on the broad range of issues will be taken into account," he said.

Jackson said he and Henderson also met with Reed Hundt, chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, to complain about a "radical dropoff" in the number of radio and television stations owned by minorities after they increased under Republican presidents Ronald Reagan and George Bush.

"We're now looking at the resegregation of ownership of media...A very small group of industrial owners now are beginning to own all the radio and TV stations...We must have some moratorium on the present process," Jackson said.
